guide.title: SoHo, Manhattan: Cast-Iron Blocks the Artists Saved
guide.intro: SoHo takes its name from a 1962 planning study — urban planner Chester Rapkin's 'The South Houston Industrial Area,' known as the Rapkin Report — but the ground beneath it has cycled through identities for three centuries. Colonial-era farmland here was part of a grant to freed Black settlers of the Dutch West India Company, and by the mid-1800s the same streets had become New York's dry-goods and textile hub, filled with masonry and cast-iron loft buildings. When wholesale trade moved out after World War II, the empty factories left an area so desolate New Yorkers nicknamed it Hell's Hundred Acres. Robert Moses wanted to run an elevated expressway straight through it in the 1960s; preservationists and the artists who had quietly moved into the vacant lofts stopped him. A 1971 zoning change legalized their live-work lofts, the 1982 Loft Law secured their tenancy, and in 1973 the city landmarked the SoHo-Cast Iron Historic District — about 500 buildings now called the world's greatest concentration of cast-iron architecture.

sections.heading: Hell's Hundred Acres to Historic District
sections.body: SoHo's cast-iron blocks were built for commerce, not looks: mid-19th-century dry-goods and textile firms favored the material because cast-iron facades could be prefabricated cheaply and cast to mimic carved stone. After the wholesale trade left following World War II, the abandoned factories sat empty at night and earned the neighborhood its "Hell's Hundred Acres" nickname through the 1950s. Robert Moses's proposed Lower Manhattan Expressway would have demolished much of it in the 1960s, but preservationists and the artists already colonizing the lofts defeated the plan. The roughly 26-block, 500-building SoHo-Cast Iron Historic District was designated by the city in 1973, extended in 2010, and named a National Historic Landmark in 1978 — sparing the very buildings Moses meant to level.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: SoHo has no station at its core but is ringed by local stops on four different lines: the N/R/W at Prince Street, the 6 at Spring Street (Lexington Avenue line), the C/E at Spring Street (Eighth Avenue line), and the 1 at Houston Street (with the 2 stopping there late nights only). Because these are all local stations, express trains like the A and the daytime Q roll past without stopping — plan around the local lines above.

sections.heading: Loft Law Legacy
sections.body: The artists who moved into SoHo's empty manufacturing lofts in the 1960s worked outside the law until a 1971 zoning amendment created "Joint Live-Work Quarters for Artists," formally legalizing artist residency in commercial buildings. The 1982 Loft Law then gave those tenants rent protection and stability. One of the best-preserved examples is 101 Spring Street, the five-story 1870 cast-iron building Donald Judd bought in 1968 as his home and studio — restored and opened for public visits in 2013, it still holds his artwork and furniture exactly as he placed them.

faq.question: How do I get to SoHo by subway?
faq.answer: Take the N/R/W to Prince Street, the 6 to Spring Street (Lexington Ave line), the C/E to Spring Street (Eighth Ave line), or the 1 to Houston Street (2 late nights only) — all local stops ringing the neighborhood's edges.

faq.question: Where does the name SoHo come from?
faq.answer: It stands for "South of Houston Street," coined in 1962 by urban planner Chester Rapkin in his study "The South Houston Industrial Area," known as the Rapkin Report.

faq.question: Why does SoHo have so many cast-iron buildings?
faq.answer: Mid-19th-century dry-goods and textile merchants built with cast-iron facades because the material could be prefabricated and cast to mimic carved stone cheaply. About 500 of those buildings survive within the SoHo-Cast Iron Historic District, landmarked in 1973 and named a National Historic Landmark in 1978.

faq.question: Can you visit Donald Judd's SoHo house?
faq.answer: Yes — 101 Spring Street, the cast-iron building Judd bought in 1968, was restored and opened for guided public visits in June 2013 through the Judd Foundation, with his artwork and furniture in place.

faq.question: Is SoHo still an artists' neighborhood?
faq.answer: The 1982 Loft Law gave the artists who colonized SoHo's lofts in the 1960s rent protection and stability, and that live-work legacy is still visible in buildings like 101 Spring Street, even as the neighborhood has become a retail and gallery district.

places.summary: A five-story 1870 cast-iron building that Donald Judd bought in 1968 as his home and studio, where he first developed his concept of permanent installation. Restored and opened for public visits in June 2013, with his artwork and furniture in place.

places.name: The Drawing Center
places.summary: A museum devoted to drawing and works on paper, at 35 Wooster Street in a 19th-century cast-iron building. Its stated mission is to present drawing as "primary, dynamic, and relevant to contemporary culture," and its exhibitions have featured drawings by tattoo artists, chefs, novelists and prisoners alongside visual artists.
places.history: Founded in 1977 by Martha Beck, a former assistant curator of drawings at the Museum of Modern Art, in a ground-floor warehouse space at 137 Greene Street; it moved to 35 Wooster Street in 1987. A $10 million renovation designed by Claire Weisz of WXY Architecture & Urban Design was completed in 2012, expanding the museum to two and a half floors and roughly 50% more exhibition space. Laura Hoptman, a former MoMA curator, was appointed executive director in 2018, when stated annual attendance was about 55,000; first-year attendance in 1977 was reported at 125,000.

places.name: Leslie-Lohman Museum of Art
places.summary: A museum dedicated to the collection, stewardship, and presentation of art by queer artists, at 26 Wooster Street. Its permanent collection holds more than 1,300 pieces among over 22,000 objects owned, including works by David Hockney, Andy Warhol and Robert Mapplethorpe. Open Wednesday to Sunday, noon to 6 p.m., with a suggested $10 donation.
places.history: The museum grew out of the Leslie-Lohman Gay Art Foundation, established by J. Frederic "Fritz" Lohman and Charles W. Leslie, who mounted their first gay art exhibition in 1969 at their Prince Street loft. Their commercial gallery closed in the early 1980s during the AIDS epidemic; the foundation applied for nonprofit status in 1987 and was granted it in 1990, a process during which the IRS objected to the word "gay" in its name. From a first permanent home in a basement at 127B Prince Street it moved to a ground-floor gallery at 26 Wooster Street in 2006, and expanded in 2016-17. The New York State Board of Regents granted it museum status in 2011, it was accredited as a museum in 2016, and it is a member of the American Alliance of Museums.

places.name: SoHo-Cast Iron Historic District
places.address: Roughly bounded by Houston, Crosby, Canal and West Broadway (26 blocks along Broadway, Greene, Mercer, and Wooster Streets)
places.summary: Approximately 500 buildings comprising what's been called the world's greatest concentration of cast-iron architecture. A New York City landmark district since 1973, extended in 2010, and a National Historic Landmark since 1978.

places.name: Balthazar
places.summary: A French brasserie in a former tannery building at 80 Spring Street, serving traditional French fare from breakfast through supper every day, with brunch at weekends and bread and pastries baked at Balthazar Bakery. Steak frites is the most popular dish, at about 200 portions a day, alongside steak au poivre, short ribs, duck confit and French onion soup — the soup the New York Daily News rated the city's second-best in 2013.
places.history: Opened on April 21, 1997 by restaurateur Keith McNally. A London sibling followed in Covent Garden in 2012, and Morandi and Minetta Tavern are its New York sister restaurants.

places.name: Dominique Ansel Bakery
places.address: 189 Spring Street (between Sullivan & Thompson), New York, NY 10012
places.summary: The Spring Street bakery where the Cronut, a croissant-donut hybrid, was created in 2013 — a pastry Time named one of the best inventions of that year. Other signatures are the DKA (Dominique's Kouign Amann), cannelés, cookie shots and rotating tarts. It sells in person and by pre-order pickup, and offers nationwide shipping, delivery and catering.
places.history: Chef Dominique Ansel opened the bakery at 189 Spring Street in 2011. Born in Beauvais, France in 1978, he spent roughly eight years at Fauchon in Paris, moved to the United States in 2006, and worked six years as executive pastry chef at Daniel Boulud's restaurant Daniel. He won the James Beard Award for Best Pastry Chef in the U.S. in 2014, was named World's Best Pastry Chef by The World's 50 Best Restaurants in 2017 — reportedly the first American to take that award — and holds France's Ordre du Mérite Agricole. Later ventures include Dominique Ansel Workshop (2021), a Las Vegas location, and Papa d'Amour (2025).

places.name: Lure Fishbar
places.address: 142 Mercer Street (at Prince Street), New York, NY
places.summary: A basement-level seafood restaurant at 142 Mercer Street, fitted out on a retro yacht theme. The menu runs from a raw bar and market-fresh sushi through crispy rice dishes, Asian red snapper, crab uni bucatini, prime steaks and a signature burger; Preston Clark is the chef. Time Out lists hours as Monday to Thursday 11:30 a.m. to 11 p.m., Friday and Saturday 11:30 a.m. to midnight, and Sunday 11:30 a.m. to 10 p.m., with an average main course around $26.
places.history: The restaurant opened in 2004. It is operated by Mercer Street Hospitality, the group entrepreneur John McDonald founded in 1993, which also runs a Lure Fishbar in Chicago at 616 North Rush Street.

places.name: The Mercer
places.address: 147 Mercer Street (at Prince Street), New York, NY 10012
places.summary: A hotel of 73 guest rooms across six floors, roughly 84,000 square feet in all, with interiors by the Parisian designer Christian Liaigre. Sartiano's is the restaurant on site, with an open kitchen, a Carrara marble bar and Hollywood-style banquettes, and Alfred Portale as culinary lead. Its sister property is The Greenwich Hotel.
places.history: The building went up in 1890 as office space for the Astor family holdings of John Jacob Astor III, designed by William Schickel, an architect known for his extensive work on behalf of the Archdiocese of New York, and was later used as artists' lofts and studios. BD Hotels and André Balazs acquired it in 1988 and opened the hotel in 1997. Mercer Kitchen held the restaurant space from 1998 to 2022; Sartiano's opened in June 2023 under Scott Sartiano with chef Alfred Portale, and the Submercer lounge reopened in 2024.

places.name: Soho Grand Hotel
places.summary: A West Broadway hotel whose venues include the Grand Bar & Salon, with DJs spinning vinyl Wednesday through Saturday; the Club Room, for live music; the Soho Diner; Gilligan's; and The Gallery. Guest bike rentals are complimentary. Interiors are by William Sofield, and the architecture incorporates bottle glass and cast-iron molding of the kind prominent in SoHo's industrial-era buildings.
places.history: The hotel opened on August 4, 1996 on the former site of the Church of St. Alphonsus Liguori, after eight earlier attempts to build a hotel there had failed over the preceding decade. David Helpern was the architect. It is owned and operated by Leonard N. Stern of Hartz Mountain Industries through GrandLife Hotels, which also operates the Roxy Hotel, and it has been featured in The Sopranos and Sex and the City.

places.name: Crosby Street Hotel
places.summary: A Firmdale hotel at 79 Crosby Street with 86 rooms and suites spread over 11 floors, each individually designed, with interiors by Kit Kemp in what the hotel calls a playful English aesthetic. On site are the Crosby Bar, serving a relaxed brasserie menu and opening onto an ivy-laden terrace, a Sculpture Garden, a Drawing Room, a screening room and a gym.
places.history: The hotel was open and covered in the press by March 2011, when The Independent ran a piece on it. It is one of three New York properties run by Firmdale Hotels, alongside The Whitby Hotel and Warren Street Hotel; Firmdale's Kit and Tim Kemp were jointly awarded an MBE in 2012 for services to the hotel industry and charity.
